title: 12-Lead ECG Acquisition
summary: Acquiring a 12-lead electrocardiogram for cardiac rhythm and ischemia evaluation.
equipment: 12-lead ECG machine with cables and electrodes
Razor (to shave excess hair if needed)
steps: Verify order. Explain procedure to patient. Ensure privacy.
Position patient supine. Expose chest and all four extremities.
Perform hand hygiene and don gloves.
Prep skin: clean and dry electrode sites with alcohol swabs. Shave excess hair if present — electrode contact is critical.
Apply limb leads to fleshy part of extremities (avoid bony prominences):
RA (white) — right arm. LA (black) — left arm. RL (green) — right leg. LL (red) — left leg.
Apply precordial leads:
V1: 4th intercostal space, right sternal border.
V2: 4th intercostal space, left sternal border.
V3: Diagonal between V2 and V4.
V4: 5th intercostal space, midclavicular line.
V5: Anterior axillary line, same level as V4.
V6: Midaxillary line, same level as V4–V5.
Instruct patient to lie still, breathe normally, and not talk.
Acquire ECG tracing. Check for artifact or loose leads — repeat if needed.
Remove electrodes and clean gel from skin.
Document time of acquisition and deliver tracing to ordering provider promptly.
nursing_considerations: STEMI is a time-critical emergency — door-to-ECG goal is ≤10 minutes for chest pain patients.
Correct lead placement is critical — misplacement leads to false positives/negatives.
Baseline wander, movement, and loose electrodes cause artifact — reapply if needed.
Right-sided ECG (V3R–V6R) ordered when right ventricular MI suspected.
For female patients, place V3–V6 under the breast, not on top of it.

title: Continuous Cardiac Monitor / Telemetry Setup
summary: Applying a 5-lead telemetry system for continuous cardiac rhythm monitoring.
steps: Verify order for continuous cardiac monitoring.
Explain procedure to patient. Perform hand hygiene and don gloves.
Assess the chest for electrode placement sites. Prep skin: clean with alcohol, dry completely. Shave area if needed.
Apply 5 electrodes (LA, RA, LL, RL, V1 or modified V1) using standard placement:
RA (white): right infraclavicular area.
LA (black): left infraclavicular area.
RL (green): lower right abdomen/torso.
LL (red): lower left abdomen/torso.
V (brown): 4th intercostal space, right sternal border (for Modified Chest Lead MCL1) or standard V1.
Attach lead wires to electrodes. Insert transmitter into the telemetry pouch. Place pouch around patient's neck or clip to gown.
Select lead for monitoring — MCL1 or Lead II most commonly used for arrhythmia detection.
Confirm signal on bedside monitor. Verify clear, artifact-free waveform with identifiable P, QRS, T.
Set monitor alarms: HR high/low, ST deviation, pause duration — per facility protocol.
Assess rhythm: rate, regularity, P waves present, PR interval, QRS width.
Change electrodes every 24–48 hours or when adhesion is poor.
Document rhythm strip, rate, intervals (PR, QRS, QTc), and alarm settings.
nursing_considerations: Proper skin prep is the #1 factor in signal quality — poor prep = artifact = false alarms = alarm fatigue.
QTc prolongation (>450 ms men; >470 ms women) is a critical finding — many medications prolong QT (amiodarone, antipsychotics, fluoroquinolones).
Alarm fatigue is a major safety hazard — set alarms to clinically meaningful limits, not default factory settings.
A continuous rhythm strip is not a substitute for a 12-lead ECG for diagnosis.
Assess for electrode site skin breakdown with each change — adhesive injury is common in frail or edematous skin.

title: Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation (CPR) / BLS
summary: Performing adult Basic Life Support (BLS) including chest compressions, rescue breaths, and AED use.
steps: STEP 1 — Scene safety: Ensure environment is safe before approaching.
STEP 2 — Assess responsiveness: Tap shoulders, shout 'Are you okay?' If no response — activate emergency response (call a code, call 911), get AED.
STEP 3 — Check breathing and pulse simultaneously for no more than 10 seconds. Gasping is not effective breathing.
STEP 4 — If no pulse: Begin high-quality chest compressions immediately.
Position: heel of hand on center of chest (lower half of sternum).
Rate: 100–120 compressions/minute.
Depth: ≥2 inches (5 cm) for adults. Do not exceed 2.4 inches.
Full chest recoil: allow complete recoil between compressions — do not lean on chest.
Minimize interruptions: <10 seconds between compression cycles.
STEP 5 — Rescue breaths (30:2 ratio without advanced airway): Provide 2 breaths over 1 second each. Visible chest rise required.
STEP 6 — Use AED as soon as available:
Power on. Apply pads (right subclavicular + left lateral chest).
Clear patient and analyze rhythm.
If shock advised: deliver shock, resume CPR immediately for 2 minutes before re-analyzing.
STEP 7 — Rotate compressor every 2 minutes to prevent fatigue.
STEP 8 — Continue until ROSC (return of spontaneous circulation), advanced providers take over, or resuscitation is discontinued.
Document: time of arrest, time CPR initiated, interventions, time of ROSC or termination.
nursing_considerations: High-quality CPR saves lives — rate (100–120/min) and depth (≥2 in) are the two most impactful factors.
Minimize pause in compressions — each pause drops perfusion pressure. Analyze, shock, resume — no delay.
If multiple rescuers: rotate compressors every 2 minutes, have one person on airway, one managing AED/defibrillation.
For hospital arrests, CPR continues until ACLS-trained team takes over — do not stop to place IV or advanced airway before compressions begin.
Push hard, push fast, allow recoil, minimize interruptions — these are the 4 pillars of quality CPR.

title: Defibrillation & Cardioversion (Assisting)
summary: Assisting with synchronized cardioversion or defibrillation for life-threatening dysrhythmias.
equipment: Conductive pads or paddles with gel
steps: Recognize the indication: VF/pulseless VT → defibrillation (unsynchronized). Unstable SVT/A-flutter/A-fib/stable VT → synchronized cardioversion.
Call for help. Activate emergency response if patient is pulseless.
Ensure IV/IO access is established. Attach continuous cardiac monitor.
Turn on defibrillator. Apply pads in anterolateral position (right subclavicular, left lateral chest) or AP position (anterior chest + left scapula).
For defibrillation (VF/pVT): select energy level (biphasic: 120–200 J for first shock, or per manufacturer; monophasic: 360 J).
For synchronized cardioversion: press SYNC button — confirm R-wave markers appear on screen. Select energy level per provider/protocol.
Charge defibrillator. Announce 'Charging!'
Confirm rhythm on monitor — confirm correct indication before delivering shock.
Announce 'All clear!' Visually sweep from head to toe. Confirm NO ONE is touching patient or bed.
Deliver shock. Immediately resume CPR for pulseless patients (do not pause to check rhythm for 2 minutes).
For cardioversion: immediately reassess rhythm and pulse after delivery.
If no conversion: repeat per ACLS/protocol at higher energy. Notify physician.
Administer antiarrhythmic medications as ordered (amiodarone, lidocaine, adenosine).
Document rhythm before/after, energy levels, number of shocks, time, patient response.
nursing_considerations: Never delay defibrillation for VF/VT — each minute without defibrillation decreases survival by 7–10%.
Synchronized cardioversion for stable VT: sedate the patient first (midazolam, propofol, etomidate as ordered) — cardioversion is extremely painful in awake patients.
Remove transdermal medication patches from chest before defibrillation — can cause burns and interfere with conduction.
Pacemakers and ICDs: place pads at least 1 inch from device, avoid placing directly over the device.
After ROSC: begin post-cardiac arrest care — targeted temperature management, coronary intervention evaluation per order.
